title: Evaluating the Cost of Conscription in the Netherlands
research_question: What is the effect of compulsory military service on the future civilian earnings of men who serve? Specifically, how much do former conscripts earn approximately ten years after service compared to members of their birth cohort who did not serve?
data_description: The analysis combines two main sources. The first, from the Dutch Defense Department, provides by birth cohort the proportion of men who actually served as conscripts, the proportion designated 'special exemption,' the proportion still 'active' (mostly in education) in 1989, and cohort size. The second source is the 'Inkomens Panel Onderzoek' from the Central Bureau for Statistics (Netherlands), which provides the mean and variance of 1989 and 1990 earnings by month-of-birth cohort, drawn as a roughly 1% random sample of Social Security records covering about 95% of men in the relevant cohorts. The unit of observation is the month-of-birth cohort. The baseline estimation sample covers cohorts born January 1956 through December 1966, with extensions in sensitivity analyses. Earnings are not top-coded and are observed in 1989 guilders.
institutional_context: Throughout most of the 20th century, the Netherlands relied on compulsory military conscription, with conscripts comprising about half of armed forces personnel and serving roughly 14 months. By law, all able-bodied men were obligated to serve, but only about 36% of a typical birth cohort actually served due to a complex set of medical, psychological, educational, breadwinner, and conscientious-objector exemptions. During the late 1970s and 1980s, two policy-driven shifts generated substantial variation in aggregate enrollment rates across birth cohorts: the entire 1959 cohort was exempted from service following a change in the age of medical examination, and beginning in 1958 the government introduced a 'special exemption' category, designating each year additional groups of medically fit men as not subject to call-up in order to match a roughly constant target number of recruits to a fluctuating supply of eligible men.
